questions.question: How does a browser turn a URL into a rendered page?
questions.title: From URL to rendered page
questions.direct_answer: A browser resolves and fetches the requested resource, parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, runs eligible scripts, calculates styles, builds the visible rendering data, performs layout, paints, and composites the result. These stages can overlap rather than forming one rigid queue.

interviewer_intent.testing: A connected mental model of navigation, parsing, and rendering.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reciting a fixed pipeline that ignores caching, streaming, script blocking, or later incremental updates.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: The exact network and rendering implementation varies by browser; developer-facing guarantees matter more than invented engine details.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Navigation resolves or reuses a connection and requests the resource.
HTML and CSS are parsed into the DOM and CSSOM.
Scripts can read or change those models and may affect parsing order.
Style, layout, paint, and compositing produce the visible result.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Loading a page begins with navigation. The browser resolves the URL, checks relevant caches and policies, establishes or reuses a connection, and requests the main resource; redirects or a service worker may alter that path.

As response bytes arrive, the HTML parser builds the DOM and discovers subresources. CSS is parsed into the CSSOM, and scripts run according to their placement and attributes, sometimes pausing parsing or changing the DOM.

The rendering engine matches styles to visible content, calculates sizes and positions during layout, records drawing work during paint, and composites the result to the screen. The browser can show useful content before every resource has finished.

For example, a render-blocking stylesheet can delay the first styled render, while a deferred script downloads during parsing and executes after parsing before `DOMContentLoaded`.

This is a dependency graph rather than one long waterfall. Performance work should identify the measured bottleneck—network, JavaScript, styles, layout, or paint—before changing code.

sections.title: Navigation and rendering overlap
sections.content: Streaming lets parsing begin before the full HTML response arrives, and resource discovery can start additional fetches while the main document is still downloading. Browser caches, priorities, connection reuse, and preload scanning all affect timing. The user sees milestones produced by this overlapping work rather than a single “page loaded” instant.

sections.title: The critical rendering dependencies
sections.content: The first render needs enough DOM and style information to describe visible content. Synchronous classic scripts can pause the HTML parser because they may inspect or modify what has already been parsed. CSS can also delay script execution when the script may depend on computed styles. After the initial frame, changes usually revisit only the affected parts of style, layout, paint, or compositing.

sections.title: Main dependencies
sections.content:
URL
 ↓ navigation, cache, connection, request
HTML bytes → DOM ─────────┐
                          ├→ style calculation → layout → paint → composite
CSS bytes  → CSSOM ───────┘
        scripts can read or change both models

sections.title: Load behaviour expressed in markup
sections.content:
```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="app.css">
<script defer src="app.js"></script>
<main>Useful content can be parsed while app.js downloads.</main>
```
The deferred classic script runs after parsing and before `DOMContentLoaded`.

questions.question: What are style recalculation, layout, paint, and compositing?
questions.title: Browser rendering work
questions.direct_answer: Style recalculation resolves which CSS values apply, layout computes geometry, paint records how pixels should look, and compositing assembles painted layers into a frame. A change may trigger some of these stages, not necessarily all of them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of browser rendering costs and how to investigate them.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling every visual update a reflow or claiming transform and opacity always run for free.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Browsers optimize aggressively, so performance conclusions require traces on the target page and device.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Style recalculation resolves CSS for affected elements.
Paint creates drawing records for visual details.
Compositing combines available layers into the final frame.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Browser rendering work is commonly described as style, layout, paint, and compositing. Style recalculation resolves the CSS values that apply, layout computes element geometry, paint records visual details, and compositing places available layers into a frame.

The stages are related but a change does not always repeat all of them. Updating an element's width can affect layout and later painting, while changing a paint-only property may leave geometry unchanged.

For example, an animation using `transform: translateX(...)` can often update during compositing without recalculating document layout. That can be smoother than animating `left`, but layer creation, memory, surrounding effects, and browser decisions still matter.

Reading geometry immediately after a write can force the browser to make pending layout information current. Repeating that read-write pattern in a loop can create layout thrashing.

The reliable approach is to group related reads and writes, keep per-frame work small, and confirm the actual stages in a browser performance trace rather than relying on a property list.

sections.title: Geometry and drawing are different costs
sections.content: Layout answers where boxes are and how large they are. Paint answers how their backgrounds, text, borders, shadows, and other details appear. Compositing can move or blend already prepared surfaces. Separating these jobs explains why two animations with the same visual distance can have very different main-thread work.

sections.title: How layout thrashing appears
sections.content: Browsers normally postpone and combine rendering work. A style write marks information as dirty; a later geometry read such as `getBoundingClientRect()` may require current layout, so the browser resolves pending work immediately. Alternating those operations for many nodes defeats batching. Reading all required measurements first and then applying all writes gives the engine more room to process one coherent update.

sections.title: What each stage decides
sections.content:
| Stage | Main question | Example trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Style | Which CSS values apply? | Add a class |
| Layout | Where and how large? | Change width or content flow |
| Paint | What should it look like? | Change background or shadow |
| Composite | How are surfaces combined? | Move an eligible transformed layer |
